Is the Treasury convenience yield rebounding?Posted on October 15, 2026

SHARE THIS PAGE:

Link Copied

The takeaway
The spread between AAA corporate bonds and Treasuries has widened since October 2025, suggesting a partial recovery in the Treasury convenience yield.
The details
US Treasury securities offer investors benefits beyond their interest payments, including safety and the ability to trade easily. Investors’ willingness to accept lower yields in exchange for these benefits is known as the Treasury convenience yield.
The FRED graph shows one proxy for this convenience yield: the option-adjusted spread of the ICE BofA AAA U.S. Corporate Index. This measure compares yields on the highest-rated corporate bonds with a Treasury yield curve, adjusting for options embedded in the corporate bonds. Since April 2026, FRED has limited this series to the most recent three years of observations, so we turn to an earlier analysis for historical context.
A post from October 2025 documented a decline in the spread over the preceding years. It averaged 67 basis points during 2012-19, compared with 36 basis points from the beginning of 2025 through October 8, 2025. The green dashed line marks the spread’s value on that date: 30 basis points, or 0.30 percentage points.
Since then, the spread has widened, although unevenly. It reached 45 basis points in March 2026, narrowed to 32 basis points in May, and rose to 46 basis points in July. On September 25, it stood at 41 basis points: 11 basis points above the October 2025 benchmark, but still below the 2012-19 average.
These movements suggest a partial recovery in the Treasury convenience yield. However, the spread also reflects corporate credit risk and liquidity conditions, so its increase cannot be attributed entirely to changes in the benefits of holding Treasuries.
How this graph was created: Search FRED for "AAA Corporate Spread" and the relevant series should be the first. Click on "Edit Graph" and open the "Add Line" tab. Click on "Create user-defined line" and add a horizontal line at 0.30.
Suggested by Julian Kozlowski and Nicholas Sullivan.
